# What this is

**What we are doing.** An advertiser pays every time its ad is shown, but
earns only when someone clicks. If we can predict **which impressions are
likely to turn into a click**, the ad can go to the right people, in the
right spot on the page, and less money is wasted. In week 9 you saw the
full classifier recipe on exactly this problem. This week you run it
yourselves, in groups, end to end.

One addition, and it is the point of the week: **an analysis is useless
until someone acts on it**. So this time the deliverable is not a knitted
report. It is a short slide deck, built as if you were pitching the model
to the marketing VP who decides whether it goes live. On Thursday a few
groups, drawn at random, present theirs to the class. The VP is smart but
has never heard the words "recall" or "AUC". Your job is to make them
understand, and to tell them what to do.

**Logistics.**

- Work in your **project groups**, laptops out, both sessions
- **Tuesday:** the analysis (Part 1)
- **Thursday:** finish the slides (Part 2), then **about three groups,
  drawn at random, present** (Part 3): about 5 minutes per group
- Every group has their slides ready as a **PDF** by the time
  presentations start on Thursday: you will not know in advance whether
  you are the one presenting

# The data

One row per ad impression, 5,000 impressions:
[`ad_click_data.csv`](https://github.com/dadepro/mkt566/raw/main/w10/data/ad_click_data.csv)
(the data you saw in the classifiers week). Put it in a fresh folder and
work in an R script or an R Markdown file.

| Column | What it is |
|---|-----------|
| `click` | the outcome: 1 if the user clicked the ad, 0 if not |
| `device` | mobile or desktop |
| `ad_position` | where the ad sat on the page: top, middle, or bottom |
| `user_segment` | new or returning visitor |
| `pages_viewed` | how many pages the user viewed in the session |
| `time_on_site` | seconds spent on the site |
| `topic_match` | 1 if the ad topic matches the page content, 0 if not |
| `past_ctr_hi` | 1 if the user clicked ads often in the past, 0 if not |

# Part 1: The analysis (Tuesday)

Run the full recipe from the classifiers week. Use **seed 123 and a 70/30
train/test split** so every group's numbers are comparable.

1. **Load and explore.** What is the baseline click rate (the share of
   impressions with a click)?
2. **Split** into training (70%) and test (30%). Fit everything on the
   training set; compute every metric on the test set.
3. **Fit a logit** of `click` on the **two features you think predict
   clicks best**: your call, argue about it in the group before you run
   anything. Then fit a second logit that **uses all the features**.
   Compare the two on test AUC and keep the better one as "your model"
4. **Classify at 0.5** and build the confusion matrix on the test set:
   the four counts, then accuracy, precision, recall, and F1
5. **Draw the ROC curve** and compute the AUC
6. **Odds ratios**, as an ordered bar chart, intercept dropped, dashed
   line at 1: which features move the odds of a click, and by how much?
7. **Pick the threshold for the business goal.** The goal, the same for
   every group: the ad team wants **at least 75% precision** (3 of every
   4 impressions you flag should be real clickers), while keeping recall
   as high as possible. Raising the threshold buys precision by throwing
   away recall, so that means finding the **lowest** threshold that
   clears the 75% bar. Report your threshold, the precision you reach,
   and the recall it leaves you compared to the 0.5 cutoff

The
[exercise handout](https://raw.githack.com/dadepro/mkt566/main/w10/case/w10-predicting-ad-click-vibecoding.html)
spells out the same tasks with questions at every step, still with no code
given. As always, your AI assistant is allowed and
encouraged.

# Part 2: The slides (Thursday)

At most **6 slides** (plus a title slide), built for the VP, not for us.
Any tool you like: PowerPoint, Google Slides, Keynote, or Quarto if you
are feeling brave. A slide a minute is a good pace for a 5-minute talk.

1. **The problem.** Why predict clicks at all, what the baseline click
   rate is in this data, and what the company would do differently if the
   model works
2. **The model.** What goes in, what comes out, and the one chart that
   shows what matters (the odds-ratio bar chart works well). Two
   takeaways in plain words: "an ad at the top of the page is about X
   times more likely to be clicked" beats "the coefficient is 0.9"
3. **How good is it.** The confusion matrix counts at the 0.5 cutoff, and
   accuracy, precision, and recall translated into plain words: "of the
   impressions we flag, X% really click; we catch Y% of all real clickers"
4. **The dial.** The business goal (75% precision while losing as little
   recall as possible), the threshold that meets it, and the trade-off:
   what you gain and what you give up compared to the 0.5 cutoff
5. **The proof.** The ROC curve with the AUC, and one sentence on what
   that number means
6. **The recommendation.** Should the ad team use this model? What is the
   one thing that could go wrong (one honest limitation)?

**Rules for the slides:**

- **No code on slides.** The VP does not read R
- Every number on a slide must come from **your own output**, and you
  should be able to show the line of code that produced it if asked
- Charts have titles and labeled axes; no screenshot of a raw R console
- Plain words before jargon: if a term from class appears, the slide (or
  you) must say what it means

# Part 3: The presentation (Thursday)

- Not every group presents: I will draw **about three groups at random**
  when presentations start, so every group must be ready
- About **5 minutes per group**, then one or two questions from me or the
  class
- **Anyone in the group can get a question.** Everyone should understand
  every slide, including the ones they did not make
- What a good talk sounds like: one idea per slide, numbers interpreted
  rather than read out loud, and a clear answer to "so what should we do?"

# If you finish early

- **Find the best pair of features.** With 7 features there are only 21
  possible pairs. Fit a logit on every pair (a loop, or your AI assistant,
  makes this quick) and compare them on test AUC. Did your group's pick
  from step 3 win? How close do just two features get to the full model?
- Try a different business goal in Part 1, step 7 (say 60% precision, or
  the budget only allows targeting the top 20% of impressions) and check
  how much the threshold moves
- Compute how much money the model saves under simple assumptions: say an
  impression costs 1 cent and a click is worth 50 cents. Compare showing
  the ad to everyone vs. only above your threshold
